results.name: fives_set_mult5_target_lift
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all multiples of 5 (not all multiples of 10), yes rate on non-example multiples-of-5 targets minus yes rate on non-multiple-of-5 targets; observed > null means the model under-generalises "multiples of 5".
results.code:
# name: fives_set_mult5_target_lift
# description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all multiples of 5 (not all multiples of 10), yes rate on non-example multiples-of-5 targets minus yes rate on non-multiple-of-5 targets; observed > null means the model under-generalises "multiples of 5".
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    feat = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        feat[s] = (len(ex) >= 2 and all(v % 5 == 0 for v in ex) and not all(v % 10 == 0 for v in ex), ex)
    ok = sets.map(lambda s: feat[s][0]).to_numpy(bool)
    isex = np.array([ti in feat[s][1] for s, ti in zip(sets, t)])
    base = ok & ~isex
    a = base & (t % 5 == 0); b = base & (t % 5 != 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: mult4_set_mult4_vs_other_even
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples all divisible by 4, yes rate on non-example multiple-of-4 targets minus yes rate on even non-multiple-of-4 targets; observed < null means people treat such sets as "even"/ranges more than the model's "multiples of 4" reading predicts.

# name: mult4_set_mult4_vs_other_even
# description: In sets of >=2 examples all divisible by 4, yes rate on non-example multiple-of-4 targets minus yes rate on even non-multiple-of-4 targets; observed < null means people treat such sets as "even"/ranges more than the model's "multiples of 4" reading predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    feat = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        feat[s] = (len(ex) >= 2 and all(v % 4 == 0 for v in ex), ex)
    ok = sets.map(lambda s: feat[s][0]).to_numpy(bool)
    isex = np.array([ti in feat[s][1] for s, ti in zip(sets, t)])
    base = ok & ~isex
    a = base & (t % 4 == 0); b = base & (t % 2 == 0) & (t % 4 != 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: final_digit_with_outlier_yes
results.description: In sets of >=3 examples where all but exactly one share a final digit, yes rate on non-example targets ending in that majority digit; observed > null means people tolerate an off-rule example more than the model's fixed 0.1 noise allows (observed < null: less).

results.name: mixed_parity_outside_range_yes
results.description: In sets of >=3 examples with both odd and even members, yes rate on targets outside [min,max] of the examples; observed > null means people guess/extend broadly when no rule fits more than the model's interval fallback and lapse predict.
results.code:
# name: mixed_parity_outside_range_yes
# description: In sets of >=3 examples with both odd and even members, yes rate on targets outside [min,max] of the examples; observed > null means people guess/extend broadly when no rule fits more than the model's interval fallback and lapse predict.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    feat = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        ex = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        mixed = len(ex) >= 3 and len({v % 2 for v in ex}) == 2
        feat[s] = (mixed, min(ex), max(ex))
    ok = sets.map(lambda s: feat[s][0]).to_numpy(bool)
    lo = sets.map(lambda s: feat[s][1]).to_numpy(int)
    hi = sets.map(lambda s: feat[s][2]).to_numpy(int)
    m = ok & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[m].mean())

results.name: single_example_near_target_yes
results.description: For single-example sets, yes rate on non-example targets within 5 of the example; observed < null means the model over-generalises to numerically close numbers from one example (observed > null: under-generalises).
results.code:
# name: single_example_near_target_yes
# description: For single-example sets, yes rate on non-example targets within 5 of the example; observed < null means the model over-generalises to numerically close numbers from one example (observed > null: under-generalises).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~sets.str.contains(",").to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    ex = pd.to_numeric(sets.where(single, "-1000"), errors="coerce").fillna(-1000).astype(int).to_numpy()
    dist = np.abs(t - ex)
    m = single & (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 5)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[m].mean())

results.name: prime_set_odd_composite_yes
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples that are all prime, yes rate on odd composite (non-prime, >1) targets; observed > null means the model's prime-over-odd preference suppresses "odd" readings too strongly after prime sets (observed < null: not strongly enough).
